headline: High-risk filesystem and shell overlap: xonsh can read/write and execute broadly while EMQX can egress broadly, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage and cascading misuse.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: xonsh can read the filesystem and process stdin/stdout, while EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress. A shared file or piped output could carry attacker-controlled instructions into xonsh, but there is no documented direct bridge or MCP channel, so this is an inferred default-pathway risk rather than a proven one.
conditions: IF EMQX output is copied into xonsh stdin or a shared file without sanitization, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF an operator wires EMQX HTTP responses into xonsh command evaluation, attacker-controlled content can steer execution.
mitigations: Disable automatic piping from EMQX outputs into xonsh.
Review any shared files before xonsh reads them.
Use allowlisted command templates in xonsh.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between EMQX outputs and xonsh inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: xonsh can read filesystem contents and broad environment variables, and EMQX touches IoT data while also having broad network egress. If they share a workspace or secrets-bearing files, xonsh can expose data that EMQX may transmit outward. The pair lacks explicit isolation or secret-handling controls, so leakage is plausible in default operator setups.
conditions: IF EMQX and xonsh share a filesystem or workspace, xonsh can read data EMQX can later exfiltrate.
IF IoT data or environment variables are placed in shared files, xonsh can surface them into networked outputs.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for EMQX and xonsh.
Remove secrets from shared directories.
Restrict xonsh read access to only required paths.
Audit outbound destinations for both agents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent network egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: xonsh has write_filesystem, execute_shell, and spawn_subprocesses, while EMQX has broad network egress and HTTP API access. Even though EMQX is not documented as writing files, the pair still creates a dangerous overlap on mutable resources if they share a directory or orchestrated state. Uncertainty about hidden write paths should be resolved upward, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory, xonsh can overwrite artifacts EMQX relies on.
IF EMQX writes or rotates files through an external workflow, xonsh shell actions can race with it.
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent.
Run xonsh under a non-shared user account.
Lock shared files before xonsh edits them.
Avoid concurrent runs against the same workspace.
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transactional state management.

D_cascading_error.rationale: xonsh can execute shell commands and subprocesses, so if it consumes EMQX-generated text as authoritative instructions or facts, downstream actions can be wrong at scale. EMQX can emit networked outputs, but there is no direct evidence of verification between the agents. The pathway exists in default operator workflows, though not necessarily by default in the software itself.
conditions: IF xonsh parses EMQX output as commands or trusted facts, errors can cascade into shell actions.
IF EMQX output is used to generate scripts or notebooks without review, downstream mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Require human review before executing EMQX-derived commands.
Log and diff EMQX outputs before xonsh consumes them.
Use read-only handoff files between agents.
Add validation checks for any generated shell content.
requires-engineering: insert schema validation before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while xonsh handles filesystem contents, configuration, and environment variables. If regulated IoT or personal data is stored in shared files, xonsh may process it under a different retention or residency regime than EMQX. No specific certification mismatch is documented, so this is a policy-mismatch risk rather than a proven violation.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is written to shared files, xonsh may process it outside EMQX's intended controls.
IF the deployment has residency or retention rules for IoT data, mixed handling can create a compliance gap.
mitigations: Classify IoT data before sharing it with xonsh.
Keep regulated data out of shared directories.
Document retention rules for both agents.
Review outbound endpoints for residency issues.
requires-engineering: align logging and retention policies across both agents.
